I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Sincerely,
Myra Schegloff
1 Village Pkwy 
Santa Monica, CA

I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Sincerely,
Michael Madden
50 Germonds Rd 
New City, NY

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Sincerely,

Aberdeen, NJ

I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Sincerely,
Gene Ammarell
12222 Pete Smith Rd 
Athens, OH

I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Sincerely,
Cheryl Henley
1203 Washington St 
Evanston, IL

I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

I learned from Food and Water Watch that LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Sincerely,
Mark Silverman
3640 S 23rd St 
Milwaukee, WI

I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Sincerely,
John Jackson
5405 Dahlen Dr 
Madison, WI

I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Sincerely,
Julie Smith
1048 Bay Oaks Dr 
Los Osos, CA

I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Sincerely,
Steve Breyman
605 Linthicum St 
Rockville, MD

I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Sincerely,
Patricia Blevins
1248 Bryan Ave 
San Jose, CA

I strongly support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I fully oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Sincerely,
William April
310 Mountain View Dr 
Waterbury Ctr, VT

Title: Comment from Paul Gravunder
Comment:

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Sincerely,
Myriam EYTHRIB
2228 W Ironwood Dr 
Chandler, AZ

I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Sincerely,
Arthur & Jean Manoogian
128 W Mariposa 
San Clemente, CA

Title: Comment from Kathleen Eaton
Comment:
NO NO NO !
I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. --LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. --There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

The transport of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) has long been prohibited by the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) from transport by rail car to protect public safety. Companies plan to transport LNG in “unit trains”, which consist of LNG in up to 100 cars. An accident or incident that released LNG would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

An unignited ground-hugging vapor cloud can move far distances,[5] and exposure to the extremely cold vapor can cause severe freeze burns. If in an enclosed space, it asphyxiates, causing death[6].

Often, these fires persist until they have exhausted all the available gas.  And in an LNG-by-rail scenario, that means tens of thousands of gallons at minimum. And even if luck provides against a fire or explosion, LNG spills can still endanger the people nearby because LNG vapor clouds displace breathable air.  Imagine the catastrophe in a populated region and around vulnerable and essential infrastructure.
An LNG release can cause a Boiling Liquid Expanding Vapor Explosion.[8] When the gas or vapor cloud in the container is released, because it is flammable it is likely to ignite after the BLEVE, typically causing a fireball that burns fast, hot and wide. A fuel air explosion can also occur, known as a “vapor cloud explosion”. A vapor cloud explosion is the mechanism used in a thermobaric weapon that uses air to generate a high-temperature explosion, producing a long duration blast wave.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment: There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by rail car. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG. The projects under construction and in process of permitting add so much more LNG that a glut of U.S. LNG could turn capital investments into stranded assets. None of these projects require LNG transport by rail car because the practice is to bring in fossil gas in a gaseous state, then liquefy it at the export terminal, loading into marine vessels for export. There is also a downside to the increase in LNG exports for domestic users. “As LNG exports have grown, consumer costs for gas have spiked as well. In early 2021, winter storm Uri caused a supply shock that sent natural gas prices from $3 to $1200 per thousand cubic feet, as a Texas freeze also slashed production. Later, the invasion of Ukraine set off a price war between domestic consumers and gas exporters, sending U.S. gas prices to their highest level in a decade”.  The economic forecast for U.S. LNG exports is dim as nations turn to homegrown, sustainable and renewable sources of energy to avoid the high prices of US LNG and to obtain energy security that they can control. This forecast does not support the concept that LNG transport by rail car is needed or justified.

Title: Comment from Lydia Garvey
Comment:
The transport of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) has long been prohibited by the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) from transport by rail car to protect public safety. PHMSA holds the mission “…to manage, and reduce, the risk to people and the environment by the transport of hazardous material by rail.”[1] The Trump Administration recklessly overturned the longstanding ban on LNG by Rail (the “Trump LNG by Rail Rule”) during its first administration but, after subsequent comprehensive analysis by PHMSA, the Trump LNG by Rail Rule was suspended under the Biden Administration and ultimately defeated by a court challenge to protect public safety and the environment. PHMSA officially repealed the Trump LNG by Rail Rule in accordance with the D.C. Circuit’s ruling on June 23, 2025 as noticed in the Federal Register.[2] LNG by rail car transport is now once again banned based on ample evidence that it cannot be done safely. It should stay that way, based on facts, not brought back for political motives, as expressed in Trumps’ Executive Orders[3] which are used as rationale for this proposed rulemaking.[4]

    LNG is extremely dangerous to handle. Its transport has unique safety hazards, exposing those along rail routes to unprecedented and unjustifiable risk. LNG is highly flammable and potentially explosive. 22 LNG rail cars contain as much explosive energy as the Hiroshima bomb. Companies plan to transport LNG in “unit trains”, which consist of LNG in up to 100 cars. An accident or incident that released LNG would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

           Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development.[9] LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. This is intolerable.

    
    LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. Over the past decade, oil and gas infrastructure has been the primary source of methane releases. To produce LNG, more gas wells would be fracked, polluting Pennsylvania communities, and methane will be leaked or vented at every stage, exacerbating climate change and worsening climate and human health impacts already being visited on communities.

    There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by rail car. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG. The projects under construction and in process of permitting add so much more LNG that a glut of U.S. LNG could turn capital investments into stranded assets. None of these projects require LNG transport by rail car because the practice is to bring in fossil gas in a gaseous state, then liquefy it at the export terminal, loading into marine vessels for export. There is also a downside to the increase in LNG exports for domestic users. “As LNG exports have grown, consumer costs for gas have spiked as well. In early 2021, winter storm Uri caused a supply shock that sent natural gas prices from $3 to $1200 per thousand cubic feet, as a Texas freeze also slashed production. Later, the invasion of Ukraine set off a price war between domestic consumers and gas exporters, sending U.S. gas prices to their highest level in a decade”.  The economic forecast for U.S. LNG exports is dim as nations turn to homegrown, sustainable and renewable sources of energy to avoid the high prices of US LNG and to obtain energy security that they can control. This forecast does not support the concept that LNG transport by rail car is needed or justified.

LNG is extremely dangerous to handle. Its transport has unique safety hazards, exposing those along rail routes to unprecedented and unjustifiable risk. LNG is highly flammable and potentially explosive. 22 LNG rail cars contain as much explosive energy as the Hiroshima bomb. Companies plan to transport LNG in “unit trains”, which consist of LNG in up to 100 cars. An accident or incident that released LNG would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.
An LNG release boils furiously into a flammable vapor cloud 620 times larger than the storage container. An unignited ground-hugging vapor cloud can move far distances,[5] and exposure to the extremely cold vapor can cause severe freeze burns. If in an enclosed space, it asphyxiates, causing death[6].
LNG fires are hotter and burn more rapidly than fires caused by oil or gasoline, and they are extremely difficult to control. Often, these fires persist until they have exhausted all the available gas.  And in an LNG-by-rail scenario, that means tens of thousands of gallons at minimum. If the released LNG is ignited, a resulting pool fire is so hot that second degree burns can occur within 5 seconds for those exposed within .69 miles and 10 seconds of exposure could be fatal.[7] First responders across the country have not received the training or the resources required to confidently contain a fire resulting from an LNG rail incident. And even if luck provides against a fire or explosion, LNG spills can still endanger the people nearby because LNG vapor clouds displace breathable air. The recommended response for fire companies and first responders is to try to evacuate and let the fire burn. Imagine the catastrophe in a populated region and around vulnerable and essential infrastructure.
An LNG release can cause a Boiling Liquid Expanding Vapor Explosion.[8] When the gas or vapor cloud in the container is released, because it is flammable it is likely to ignite after the BLEVE, typically causing a fireball that burns fast, hot and wide. A fuel air explosion can also occur, known as a “vapor cloud explosion”. A vapor cloud explosion is the mechanism used in a thermobaric weapon that uses air to generate a high-temperature explosion, producing a long duration blast wave.

This is intolerable.

That derailment led to several tense days where residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. And the impacts were not just local; the accident resulted in toxic chemicals spreading to sixteen nearby states.[10] The mismanaged handling of the catastrophe has been widely criticized, including by the federal government[11] and long-term health and environmental impacts continue to be studied.[12] There is no evidence that hazardous material transport of LNG would be any more safely accomplished; in fact, the volatility, flammability, and explosive nature of LNG has the potential to result in a worse catastrophic outcome.

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Title: Comment from David Dunnell
Comment:
The transport of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) has long been prohibited by the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) from transport by rail car to protect public safety. PHMSA holds the mission “…to manage, and reduce, the risk to people and the environment by the transport of hazardous material by rail.”
LNG by rail car transport is now once again banned based on ample evidence that it cannot be done safely. It should stay that way, based on facts, not brought back for political motives, as expressed in Trumps’ Executive Orders which are used as rationale for this proposed rulemaking.
LNG is extremely dangerous to handle. Its transport has unique safety hazards, exposing those along rail routes to unprecedented and unjustifiable risk. LNG is highly flammable and potentially explosive. 22 LNG rail cars contain as much explosive energy as the Hiroshima bomb. Companies plan to transport LNG in “unit trains”, which consist of LNG in up to 100 cars. An accident or incident that released LNG would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.
An LNG release boils furiously into a flammable vapor cloud 620 times larger than the storage container. An unignited ground-hugging vapor cloud can move far distances, and exposure to the extremely cold vapor can cause severe freeze burns. If in an enclosed space, it asphyxiates, causing death.
LNG fires are hotter and burn more rapidly than fires caused by oil or gasoline, and they are extremely difficult to control. Often, these fires persist until they have exhausted all the available gas.  And in an LNG-by-rail scenario, that means tens of thousands of gallons at minimum.
First responders across the country have not received the training or the resources required to confidently contain a fire resulting from an LNG rail incident. And even if luck provides against a fire or explosion, LNG spills can still endanger the people nearby because LNG vapor clouds displace breathable air. Title: Comment from Barbara Brandom
Comment:
As a retired physician with training in public health I am commenting on PHMSA-2025-0032 focused specifically on: III. Topics Under Consideration,B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24.

The transport of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) has long been prohibited by the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) from transport by rail car to protect public safety. PHMSA holds the mission “…to manage, and reduce, the risk to people and the environment by the transport of hazardous material by rail.” The Trump Administration recklessly overturned the longstanding ban on LNG by Rail (the “Trump LNG by Rail Rule”) during its first administration but, after subsequent comprehensive analysis by PHMSA, the Trump LNG by Rail Rule was suspended under the Biden Administration and ultimately defeated by a court challenge to protect public safety and the environment. PHMSA officially repealed the Trump LNG by Rail Rule in accordance with the D.C. Circuit’s ruling on June 23, 2025 as noticed in the Federal Register. LNG by rail car transport is now once again banned based on ample evidence that it cannot be done safely. It should stay that way, based on facts, not brought back for political motives, as expressed in Trumps’ Executive Orders, which are used as rationale for this proposed rulemaking.

At present more LNG Is produced in the United States for export than for domestic use. This raises the costs for consumers of gas in the US, as has been recognized for years. At present 'the energy emergency' described by Trump exists only in the balance sheets of the extractive technology and pipeline industries and Trump's personal needs. Nations abroad are not eager to purchase LNG from the US because doing so puts them at the mercy of economic forces outside their borders. The European Union and many other countries are developing solat, wind and other non fossil fuels sources of energy because they are cheaper, faster to deploy and produce less air and water pollution, thus preserving health of people and the environment. Thus, further investment in LNG export facilitated by extremely dangerous transport of LNG by rail, creates wasted assets. The people of the United States pay for this with their tax money and at the point of purchase of gas and extracting, transporting and burning gas produces significant permanent harms to our health.

We are experiencing the beginnings of the climate crisis. One of the few actions we can take to slow the climate destabilization is tro keep gas in the ground and follow the European path to cleaner energy. The International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled on July 23, 2025, that countries have a duty to protect the environment from greenhouse gas emissions and must act with due diligence and cooperation to fulfill this obligation. 
1
 The court also stated that failure to meet these obligations could lead to legal responsibility and potential reparations. 
2 
We must not endanger our own population in the US and we must not endanger the entire world by ignoring the International Court, by allowing LNG transport by rail. There have been train derailments in and near Pittsburgh. If any of those trains included LNG that exploded the fire would burn until all fuel was exhausted. A long LNG train has the potential to produce a firestorm more powerful than the bomb dropped on Hiroshima at the end of World War 2. This must be avoided by continuing to prohibit LNG transport by rail in the USA.

Title: Comment from Judy Morgan
Comment: I urge you to continue prohibition on transport of LNG by train.  It poses an unnecessary risk to populations, schools and other buildings along the train routes.  There have been a number of serious train accidents in recent decades.  One notable one was the derailment of a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride, in East Palestine, Ohio in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days where residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion.  Derailment of a train carrying LNG would be even more serious, with the potential of an explosion, if enough cars are involved, at the level of the Horoshima atomic bomb.  Even a small number of cars could devastate a small community, with a cloud of frozen gas that would explode at the first spark.  At the same time we need to be moving away from fossil fuels, which includes fracked gas, toward clean energy, which is better for public health, can create large numbers of new jobs, and reduce the increasing threat of climate disasters.  I urge you to act responsibly in the face of all the negative factors of train transport of natural gas, especially when the US does not need to be exporting LNG abroad.  We do not want to subject US citizens to increased risk for the sake of providing cheaper power to other countries.

I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Sincerely,
Suzanne Byron
9276 Eagle Nest Dr 
Navarre, FL

Title: Comment from Chester Residents Concerned for Quality Living
Comment:
Attention PHMSA:
I am writing on behalf of Chester Residents Concerned for Quality Living (CRCQL) to voice our deep concerns around the hazards of LNG by rail and implore PHMSA to uphold the standing ban on this extremely dangerous method of transporting gas. CRCQL is a community-led non-profit based in Chester, PA that organizes around issues of clean air and health.

There are good reasons why PHMSA has long prohibited LNG by Rail and that courts agree it is a threat to public safety and the environment. There is no way LNG by rail car transport can be done safely. LNG is extremely explosive and dangerous to handle. Companies plan to transport LNG in “unit trains”, which consist of LNG in up to 100 cars. An accident or incident that released LNG would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

The community of East Palestine, Ohio is still dealing with the aftermath of the toxic train derailment that happened in 2023. If the train cars had been carrying LNG, the explosion could have had the capacity of Hiroshima bomb. The derailment forced many to evacuate due to toxic chemicals burning off into the air for fear of an explosion. It has impacted the water quality in the area and many suffer from long-term health issues due to their exposure. In addition, the impacts were not just local; it resulted in toxic chemicals spreading to nearby states. The rail infrastructure in our country is outdated and not nearly as safe as it should be for the chemicals they carry today, let alone an unprecedented form of gas as volatile and explosive as LNG.

The region where the LNG by rail is being proposed comprises densely populated communities and cities and are often predominantly low-income and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. Chester City where we are located, along the Delaware River, is one of those communities. Residents are already suffering from a legacy of toxic industry, with childhood asthma rates 5x the national average. LNG by rail would further expose those living along routes to unprecedented and unjustifiable risk.

Not to mention, there is no economic benefit to the public! Export is the primary market for LNG. Transporting LNG by rail would put millions of American’s lives, homes and water at risk all for the profit of private companies selling it overseas.
PHMSA holds the mission “to manage, and reduce, the risk to people and the environment by the transport of hazardous material by rail.” PHMSA has a responsibility to the citizens of the United States of America and must uphold that charge by continuing to ban LNG by rail. The risks are simply way too high.

Sincerely, 
Erica Burman
Administrator, Chester Residents Concerned for Quality Living
ChesterPaEJ.org

Comment:
In reference  to PHMSA-2018-0025-0096 I implore  the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration to continue the ban on the rail transport of Liquid Natural Gas (LNG) The transport of LNG has long been prohibited by the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) from transport by rail car to protect public safety. The Natural Transportation Safety https://www.regulations.gov/document?D=PHMSA-2018-0025-0078 has stated that allowing liquefied natural gas to be moved in railroad tank cars “would be detrimental to public safety if LNG is transported  in rail tanks  and the  National Association of State  Fire  Marshals    (https://www.regulations.gov/document?D=PHMSA-2018-0025-0096 )   wrote  that the Federal Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration “not proposing any additional safety requirements on these rail cars, or the trains which transport them, despite the potential hazards of LNG product.”
Liquid  natural gas  obtained from fracking  wells is  cryogenically cooled to minus 260 degrees  in order for it  be stored. If it escapes from its container , it expands  600 times  its size becoming  extremely cold  and flammable vapor cloud  called a BLEVE (boiling liquified expanding vapor explosion)   - vaporizing and exploding at the same time.  It will cause asphyxiation and  freeze burns  to those in its path. Also if it ignites, it can’t  be  extinguished. 
An example of  this type  of  disaster occurred  in 1944 when LNG leaked  from a tank farm in Cleveland , Ohio  and flowed into the city's sewer system and ignited.  It  killed 131 people, injured  hundreds  and destroyed one  square mile of the city.
https://www.clevelandpolicemuseum.org/historical/east-ohio-gas-explosion-october-20-1944-police-response-and-report/ 

In regard  to  train transport, one rail car could destroy a city and  22 rail cars have the  potential force of the  Hiroshima bomb.

In addition LNG is not the future of American Energy. The majority of LNG produced is for export and there's enough for global demand for decades  acccording to The Office of Fossil Energy & Carbon Management (FECM) of the Department of Energy (DOE) 2024 Liquid natural Gas Export Study .In addition  American consumers will face  increased prices of the natural gas itself, electricity where natural gas is used to generate electricity in power plants and the increased costs of manufactured products since businesses will pass the  higher energy costs to the consumer.   Clean renewable energy is the answer
In  2018  the Sustainable Energy and Environmental Protection (SEEP) conference was held at the University of the West of Scotland, UK, The  research submitted there  and was reviewed The report concluded ” Renewable energy sources are the most affordable method for getting rid of fossil fuels, which are limited in resources and have severe environmental impacts” https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1364032122000405#preview-section-snippets
Thus  the ban for LNG rail transport should continue.

Title: Comment from Laura Overmann
Comment:
I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Sincerely,
Laura Overmann
508 El Camino Real Apt 4 
Burlingame, CA

Title: Comment from NE Forest Watch
Comment:
Commenting on PHMSA-2025-0032 focused specifically on: III. Topics Under Consideration,B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24.

The transport of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) has long been prohibited by the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) from transport by rail car to protect public safety. PHMSA holds the mission “…to manage, and reduce, the risk to people and the environment by the transport of hazardous material by rail.”[1] The Trump Administration recklessly overturned the longstanding ban on LNG by Rail (the “Trump LNG by Rail Rule”) during its first administration but, after subsequent comprehensive analysis by PHMSA, the Trump LNG by Rail Rule was suspended under the Biden Administration and ultimately defeated by a court challenge to protect public safety and the environment. PHMSA officially repealed the Trump LNG by Rail Rule in accordance with the D.C. Circuit’s ruling on June 23, 2025 as noticed in the Federal Register.[2] LNG by rail car transport is now once again banned based on ample evidence that it cannot be done safely. It should stay that way, based on facts, not brought back for political motives, as expressed in Trumps’ Executive Orders[3] which are used as rationale for this proposed rulemaking.[4]
LNG is extremely dangerous to handle. Its transport has unique safety hazards, exposing those along rail routes to unprecedented and unjustifiable risk. LNG is highly flammable and potentially explosive. 22 LNG rail cars contain as much explosive energy as the Hiroshima bomb. Companies plan to transport LNG in “unit trains”, which consist of LNG in up to 100 cars. An accident or incident that released LNG would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.
An LNG release boils furiously into a flammable vapor cloud 620 times larger than the storage container. An unignited ground-hugging vapor cloud can move far distances,[5] and exposure to the extremely cold vapor can cause severe freeze burns. If in an enclosed space, it asphyxiates, causing death[6].
LNG fires are hotter and burn more rapidly than fires caused by oil or gasoline, and they are extremely difficult to control. Often, these fires persist until they have exhausted all the available gas.  And in an LNG-by-rail scenario, that means tens of thousands of gallons at minimum. If the released LNG is ignited, a resulting pool fire is so hot that second degree burns can occur within 5 seconds for those exposed within .69 miles and 10 seconds of exposure could be fatal.[7] First responders across the country have not received the training or the resources required to confidently contain a fire resulting from an LNG rail incident. And even if luck provides against a fire or explosion, LNG spills can still endanger the people nearby because LNG vapor clouds displace breathable air. The recommended response for fire companies and first responders is to try to evacuate and let the fire burn. Imagine the catastrophe in a populated region and around vulnerable and essential infrastructure.
An LNG release can cause a Boiling Liquid Expanding Vapor Explosion.[8] When the gas or vapor cloud in the container is released, because it is flammable it is likely to ignite after the BLEVE, typically causing a fireball that burns fast, hot and wide. A fuel air explosion can also occur, known as a “vapor cloud explosion”. A vapor cloud explosion is the mechanism used in a thermobaric weapon that uses air to generate a high-temperature explosion, producing a long duration blast wave. 
Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development.[9] LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. This is intolerable.
LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days where residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. And the impacts were not just local; the accident resulted in toxic chemicals spreading to sixteen nearby states.[10] The mismanaged handling of the catastrophe has been widely criticized, including by the federal government[11] and long-term health and environmental impacts continue to be studied.[12] There is no evidence that hazardous material transport of LNG would be any more safely accomplished; in fact, the volatility, flammability, and explosive nature of LNG has the potential to result in a worse catastrophic outcome.

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. --There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Sincerely,
Gregory Penchoen
3520 Millvale Ave NE 
Canton, OH

I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Sincerely,
Richard Miller
649 C St SE APT 302 
Washington, DC

I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Sincerely,
Nagwa Ahmed-Cramer
5465 Rabbit Foot Rd 
East Stroudsburg, PA

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Title: Comment from Judith Canepa
Comment:
I am concerned about the transport of Liquefied Natural Gas by rail tank car. This is a dangerous method of transporting something that must be chilled to 261 degrees below zero, Fahrenheit, in order to transition from gas to liquid, and then kept at that temperature. If an accident occurs, or the rail tank car is damaged in some other way, and LNG is released, it not only freezes but also suffocates the lungs and bronchia of anyone in the vicinity, including first responders. And it's flammable. The disaster response would have to wait until and unless emergency equipment arrives. When and where would that happen? The first responders across the railways of the U.S. are not trained for LNG accidents. In addition, loading and unloading these cars is hazardous. If there were a release of LNG, the liquid would become a flammable vapor cloud 620 times larger than the storage container, according to your own findings (“Immediate ignition with liquid still on the ground could cause the spill to develop into a pool fire and present a radiant heat hazard. If there is no ignition source, the LNG will vaporize rapidly forming a cold gas cloud that is initially heavier than air, mixes with ambient air, spreads and is carried downwind.” P. 10 “Methane in vapor state can be an asphyxiant when it displaces oxygen in a confined space.” P. 11. SP 20534 Special Permit to transport LNG by rail in DOT-113C120W rail tank cars. Final Environmental Assessment. Docket No. PHMSA-2019-0100. December 5, 2019. P. 10.. 

An unignited ground-hugging vapor cloud can move far distances, and exposure to the extremely cold vapor can cause severe freeze burns. If in an enclosed space, it asphyxiates, causing death.

I refer you to your own study, NJDOT, Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration, Docket No. PHMSA-2018-0025 (HM-264) RIN 2137-AF40, Hazardous Materials: Liquefied Natural Gas by Rail, NPRM Preliminary Regulatory Impact Analysis, October 2019, Executive Summary

Noting that a train with 22 LNG rail cars contains as much explosive energy as the Hiroshima bomb.

I oppose lifting the ban on LNG transport by rail tank care and urge the PHMSA to remove that recommendation/request.

Title: Comment from Clean Water Action - Pennsylvania
Comment:
Benjamin D. Kochman, Acting Administrator.
U.S. Department of Transportation
Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, West Building
Ground Floor, Room W12–140,
Washington, DC 20590–0001

Mr. Kochman

On behalf of Clean Water Action, Pennsylvania, and our roughly 80,000 members across the Commonwealth, I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

We support the retention of the prohibition on the transport of LNG by railcar and urge that the ban be kept in place. 

The transportation of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) has long been prohibited by the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) from being transported by rail car, as it poses a risk to public safety. The previous attempt by the first Trump Administration to overturn the longstanding ban on LNG by Rail was suspended under the Biden Administration and ultimately defeated by the D.C. Circuit’s ruling on June 23, 2025, as noted in the Federal Register . 

LNG is extremely dangerous to handle, yet companies plan to transport LNG in “unit trains”, which consist of LNG in up to 100 cars. Its transport has unique safety hazards, exposing those along rail routes to unprecedented and unjustifiable risk. Twenty-two LNG rail cars contain as much explosive energy as the Hiroshima atomic bomb.  An accident or incident that released LNG would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

While LNG was not being transported in the train derailment that occurred in East Palestine, Ohio in 2023, the fallout from this disaster demonstrates the far reaching impact that an accident or incident can have. Pennsylvanians between 10-20 miles away in Beaver and Lawrence counties experienced health symptoms that started after the venting and burning associated with the accident released a carcinogen into the environment. Residents of these communities also had concerns with the actions taken to get the situation under control, as upstream water sources from them were contaminated with firefighting foam that contained toxic PFAS chemicals.

An LNG explosion during transport through Philadelphia and New Jersey would cause injury and death to hundreds of thousands of people and devastate the economy of the region and Pennsylvania.
