Title: Comment from Juliana  Harris
Comment:
I am writing to oppose the proposed ban reversal on LNG transport by rail. It is unsafe for the public (as demonstrated by the East Palestine incident), terrible for the environment, and unnecessary.

The transport of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) has long been prohibited by the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) from transport by rail car to protect public safety. PHMSA holds the mission “…to manage, and reduce, the risk to people and the environment by the transport of hazardous material by rail.” [Source: NJDOT, Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration, Docket No. PHMSA-2018-0025 (HM-264) RIN 2137-AF40, Hazardous Materials: Liquefied Natural Gas by Rail, NPRM Preliminary Regulatory Impact Analysis, October 2019, Executive Summary]

LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. Over the past decade, oil and gas infrastructure has been the primary source of methane releases. To produce LNG, more gas wells would be fracked, polluting Pennsylvania communities, and methane will be leaked or vented at every stage, exacerbating climate change and worsening climate and human health impacts already being visited on communities.

There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by rail car. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG. The projects under construction and in process of permitting add so much more LNG that a glut of U.S. LNG could turn capital investments into stranded assets. None of these projects require LNG transport by rail car because the practice is to bring in fossil gas in a gaseous state, then liquefy it at the export terminal, loading into marine vessels for export. There is also a downside to the increase in LNG exports for domestic users. “As LNG exports have grown, consumer costs for gas have spiked as well. In early 2021, winter storm Uri caused a supply shock that sent natural gas prices from $3 to $1200 per thousand cubic feet, as a Texas freeze also slashed production. Later, the invasion of Ukraine set off a price war between domestic consumers and gas exporters, sending U.S. gas prices to their highest level in a decade”.  The economic forecast for U.S. LNG exports is dim as nations turn to homegrown, sustainable and renewable sources of energy to avoid the high prices of US LNG and to obtain energy security that they can control. This forecast does not support the concept that LNG transport by rail car is needed or justified.

Please do not lift restrictions on LNG transport by rail car.

PHMSA officially repealed the Trump LNG by Rail Rule in accordance with the D.C. Circuit’s ruling on June 23, 2025 as noticed in the Federal Register. LNG is extremely dangerous to handle. Its transport has unique safety hazards, exposing those along rail routes to unprecedented and unjustifiable risk. LNG is highly flammable and potentially explosive. 22 LNG rail cars contain as much explosive energy as the Hiroshima bomb. Companies plan to transport LNG in “unit trains”, which consist of LNG in up to 100 cars. An accident or incident that released LNG would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.
An LNG release boils furiously into a flammable vapor cloud 620 times larger than the storage container. An unignited ground-hugging vapor cloud can move far distances, and exposure to the extremely cold vapor can cause severe freeze burns. If in an enclosed space, it asphyxiates, causing death.
LNG fires are hotter and burn more rapidly than fires caused by oil or gasoline, and they are extremely difficult to control. Often, these fires persist until they have exhausted all the available gas.  And in an LNG-by-rail scenario, that means tens of thousands of gallons at minimum. If the released LNG is ignited, a resulting pool fire is so hot that second degree burns can occur within 5 seconds for those exposed within .69 miles and 10 seconds of exposure could be fatal. First responders across the country have not received the training or the resources required to confidently contain a fire resulting from an LNG rail incident. The recommended response for fire companies and first responders is to try to evacuate and let the fire burn. Imagine the catastrophe in a populated region and around vulnerable and essential infrastructure.
An LNG release can cause a Boiling Liquid Expanding Vapor Explosion. When the gas or vapor cloud in the container is released, because it is flammable it is likely to ignite after the BLEVE, typically causing a fireball that burns fast, hot and wide. A fuel air explosion can also occur, known as a “vapor cloud explosion”. A vapor cloud explosion is the mechanism used in a thermobaric weapon that uses air to generate a high-temperature explosion, producing a long duration blast wave. 
Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. And the impacts were not just local; the accident resulted in toxic chemicals spreading to sixteen nearby states. The mismanaged handling of the catastrophe has been widely criticized, including by the federal government and long-term health and environmental impacts continue to be studied. There is no evidence that hazardous material transport of LNG would be any more safely accomplished; in fact, the volatility, flammability, and explosive nature of LNG has the potential to result in a worse catastrophic outcome.
LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis.

An LNG release boils furiously into a flammable vapor cloud 620 times larger than the storage container. An unignited ground-hugging vapor cloud can move far distances, and exposure to the extremely cold vapor can cause severe freeze burns. If in an enclosed space, it asphyxiates, causing death.

Often, these fires persist until they have exhausted all the available gas.  And in an LNG-by-rail scenario, that means tens of thousands of gallons at minimum. Title: Comment from Lisa Maragon
Comment:
I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

Title: Comment from Ralph Kisberg
Comment:
Commenting on PHMSA-2025-0032 focused specifically on: III. Topics Under Consideration,B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24.

Title: Comment from Charles Sherrouse
Comment:
The transport of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) has long been prohibited by the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) from transport by rail car to protect public safety.  The 'LNG by Rail Rule' was suspended and ultimately repealed by PHMSA on June 23, 2025, restoring the longstanding ban on LNG transport by rail which is based on ample evidence that it cannot be done safely.

LNG is extremely dangerous to handle and its transport has unique safety hazards.  A ruptured container of LNG boils furiously into a flammable vapor cloud hundreds of times larger than the storage container.  A ground-hugging vapor cloud can extend long distances.  Exposure to the extremely cold vapor can cause severe freeze burns.  LNG is highly flammable and potentially explosive.  A 'unit train' of 96 to 100 cars carries the explosive energy of four Hiroshima-scale bombs.

First responders across the country have not received the training or the resources required to handle an LNG rail incident.  An accident that released LNG would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.  Exposing communities along rail routes to such risk is unjustifiable.

LNG transport by rail is not necessary as export infrastructure is planned and built for fuels transported in a gaseous state, then liquefied at the export terminal.  A Department of Energy study published in December 2024 found that “the amounts [of LNG infrastructure] that have already been approved will be more than sufficient to meet global demand for U.S. LNG for decades to come.

The production of methane for export continues to cause contamination of aquifers, removing a vital sources of drinking water for many communities.  It has also contaminated surface steams causing severe environmental and health effects.  The cumulative leakage of methane, a potent greenhouse-effect gas, from well through transport to end use has substantial and long term contribution to dangerous warming of our global climate.  End use results in release of carbon dioxide additionally contributing substantially to the greenhouse effect.  Creating infrastructure and systems to further fossil fuel production, transport and use is neither sustainable nor justifiable.

Title: Comment from Rita  Raftery
Comment:
I am submitting this comment focused on III. Topics Under Consideration, B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (49 CFR Part 107) and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180) Section 24. 

I support the retention of the prohibition on transporting Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) by rail car and urge that the ban be kept in place. I oppose the transportation of LNG by rail car because:

--LNG is liquefied methane, which is a greenhouse gas 86 times more powerful than carbon dioxide in heating the atmosphere on a 20-year time scale and 104 times more powerful over a 10-year period, the periods of time when scientists say we must reduce GHG emissions to address the climate crisis. 

--LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads, where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days, during which residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. 

--There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by railcar. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG.

--Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. 

To prevent the worst impacts of climate change, we need to keep fracked gas out of our communities. I urge you to keep the ban on LNG transport by rail in place. Any other decision would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.

Sincerely,
Rita Raftery
99 Hobart Street 
Ridgefield Park, NJ

Title: Comment from Aaron Fumarola
Comment:
The transport of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) has long been prohibited by the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) from transport by rail car to protect public safety. PHMSA holds the mission “…to manage, and reduce, the risk to people and the environment by the transport of hazardous material by rail.” The Trump Administration recklessly overturned the longstanding ban on LNG by Rail (the “Trump LNG by Rail Rule”) during its first administration but, after subsequent comprehensive analysis by PHMSA, the Trump LNG by Rail Rule was suspended under the Biden Administration and ultimately defeated by a court challenge to protect public safety and the environment. PHMSA officially repealed the Trump LNG by Rail Rule in accordance with the D.C. Circuit’s ruling on June 23, 2025 as noticed in the Federal Register. LNG by rail car transport is now once again banned based on ample evidence that it cannot be done safely. It should stay that way, based on facts, not brought back for political motives, as expressed in Trumps’ Executive Orders which are used as rationale for this proposed rulemaking.

LNG is extremely dangerous to handle. Its transport has unique safety hazards, exposing those along rail routes to unprecedented and unjustifiable risk. LNG is highly flammable and potentially explosive. 22 LNG rail cars contain as much explosive energy as the Hiroshima bomb. Companies plan to transport LNG in “unit trains”, which consist of LNG in up to 100 cars. An accident or incident that released LNG would be catastrophic for communities and the environment.
An LNG release boils furiously into a flammable vapor cloud 620 times larger than the storage container. An unignited ground-hugging vapor cloud can move far distances, and exposure to the extremely cold vapor can cause severe freeze burns. If in an enclosed space, it asphyxiates, causing death.

LNG fires are hotter and burn more rapidly than fires caused by oil or gasoline, and they are extremely difficult to control. Often, these fires persist until they have exhausted all the available gas.  And in an LNG-by-rail scenario, that means tens of thousands of gallons at minimum. If the released LNG is ignited, the resulting pool fire is so hot that second-degree burns can occur within 5 seconds for those exposed within .69 miles, and 10 seconds of exposure could be fatal. First responders across the country have not received the training or the resources required to confidently contain a fire resulting from an LNG rail incident. And even if luck provides against a fire or explosion, LNG spills can still endanger the people nearby because LNG vapor clouds displace breathable air. The recommended response for fire companies and first responders is to try to evacuate and let the fire burn. Imagine the catastrophe in a populated region and around vulnerable and essential infrastructure.

An LNG release can cause a Boiling Liquid Expanding Vapor Explosion. When the gas or vapor cloud in the container is released, because it is flammable it is likely to ignite after the BLEVE, typically causing a fireball that burns fast, hot and wide. A fuel air explosion can also occur, known as a “vapor cloud explosion”. A vapor cloud explosion is the mechanism used in a thermobaric weapon that uses air to generate a high-temperature explosion, producing a long duration blast wave. 

Communities living near the major railways that would be used to transport LNG are predominantly low-income communities and communities of color, as a result of decades of systemic racism in siting and development. LNG by Rail adds to the unjust environmental burdens of those in harm’s way. This is intolerable.

LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days where residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. And the impacts were not just local; the accident resulted in toxic chemicals spreading to sixteen nearby states. The mismanaged handling of the catastrophe has been widely criticized, including by the federal government and long-term health and environmental impacts continue to be studied. There is no evidence that hazardous material transport of LNG would be any safer; in fact, the volatility, flammability, and explosive nature of LNG have the potential to result in a worse catastrophic outcome.

Comment:
The transport of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) has long been prohibited by the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) from transport by rail car to protect public safety. PHMSA holds the mission “…to manage, and reduce, the risk to people and the environment by the transport of hazardous material by rail.”[1] The Trump Administration recklessly overturned the longstanding ban on LNG by Rail (the “Trump LNG by Rail Rule”) during its first administration but, after subsequent comprehensive analysis by PHMSA, the Trump LNG by Rail Rule was suspended under the Biden Administration and ultimately defeated by a court challenge to protect public safety and the environment. PHMSA officially repealed the Trump LNG by Rail Rule in accordance with the D.C. Circuit’s ruling on June 23, 2025 as noticed in the Federal Register.[2] LNG by rail car transport is now once again banned based on ample evidence that it cannot be done safely. It should stay that way, based on facts, not brought back for political motives, as expressed in Trumps’ Executive Orders[3] which are used as rationale for this proposed rulemaking.[4]


There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by rail car. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG. The projects under construction and in process of permitting add so much more LNG that a glut of U.S. LNG could turn capital investments into stranded assets. None of these projects require LNG transport by rail car because the practice is to bring in fossil gas in a gaseous state, then liquefy it at the export terminal, loading into marine vessels for export. There is also a downside to the increase in LNG exports for domestic users. “As LNG exports have grown, consumer costs for gas have spiked as well. In early 2021, winter storm Uri caused a supply shock that sent natural gas prices from $3 to $1200 per thousand cubic feet, as a Texas freeze also slashed production. Later, the invasion of Ukraine set off a price war between domestic consumers and gas exporters, sending U.S. gas prices to their highest level in a decade”.  The economic forecast for U.S. LNG exports is dim as nations turn to homegrown, sustainable and renewable sources of energy to avoid the high prices of US LNG and to obtain energy security that they can control. This forecast does not support the concept that LNG transport by rail car is needed or justified.

Title: Comment from Diana Dakey
Comment:
PHMSA-2025-0050

PHMSA, in its advance notice of proposed rulemaking (ANPRM) is soliciting stakeholder feedback on “whether to repeal or amend any requirements in the Hazardous Materials Rulemaking Procedures and Program Procedures, or the Hazardous Materials Regulations to eliminate undue burdens on the identification, development, and use of domestic energy resources and to improve government efficiency.”

I am a stakeholder, and millions of people are also stakeholders by virtue of living near, working near, and traveling near freight rail lines.  Such rail lines in northeast Pennsylvania and southeast Pennsylvania were recently proposed for LNG transport by unit trains (around 100 tanker cars) of LNG. Due to the existential threat to my community, I informed myself regarding the dangers of LNG. 

Under B. Hazardous Materials Program Procedures (CFR Part 107 and Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171 Through 180, PHMSA indicates, 24. Specific to transporting liquefied natural gas (LNG) by rail tank car, PHMSA is interested in hearing from stakeholders about the possibility of any future markets for transportation of LNG by rail tank car. As such, PHMSA seeks information on the following questions. First, is there a current or potential future market for special permits to transport LNG by rail tank car?

The answer is, “No”. 

Allowing LNG transport by rail will not “improve government efficiency.”  It will do the opposite. In order to transport LNG by rail safely (not possible), regulations will be needed to address routes, unit train length, rail cars, grade crossings, crew size; notification, training, and equipping emergency responders. There will also be a need for bonding, insurance, and tribunals to allocate disaster recovery funds after a catastrophe. Nothing “efficient” about all that.  Did we not learn anything from the East Palestine disaster? 

LNG is even more hazardous than the East Palestine load. An LNG release boils furiously into a flammable vapor cloud over 600 times larger than the storage container. An unignited ground-hugging vapor can cause severe freeze burns and asphyxiation. The vaporizing methane, if it encounters any spark, can cause an uncontrollable fire and explosion. 

PHMSA is looking for how to “eliminate undue burden on the …development… of domestic energy””. LNG-for-export IS a burden on domestic energy. It does not contribute to domestic energy. By pulling supply from domestic markets, LNG increases energy costs for domestic consumers -- both households and manufacturers -- who use gas. 

At III. Topics Under Consideration, A. Procedural Regulations and Actions, 3. What regulatory amendments… could eliminate undue burdens…by improving or clarifying the scope of PHMSA’s regulatory oversight relative to that each of the other Federal agencies and State regulatory authorities?   Here is the problem: Neither Pennsylvania, nor any state, has jurisdiction over railroads: Jurisdiction is Federal. States should be given the right to be notified of future business plans for shipping of hazardous materials, and have the right to modify the route and timing or to refuse the business plan, if the state determines shipping cannot be done safely. 

For decades there was a ban on bulk shipping of LNG on the nation’s railroads. Then, in the first Trump administration, the LNG-by-rail rule was approved, despite the overwhelming amount of expert commentary advising against this move. 

There is no “energy emergency” for fossil fuels. LNG is not about energy “independence”, it's about profit for gas investors. The only true independence is renewables.  

LNG perpetuates methane and CO2 emissions here and abroad. It continues fracking and pipeline infrastructure which contribute to health problems, toxic waste, and the taking of property rights and value. 

LNG is old tech. The United States should be putting all its “energy” into wind, solar, batteries, and other nonfossil fuels and technologies. That is what we should be exporting for “dominance”. That is what China is doing. 

The D.C. Circuit Court vacated the LNG-by-Rail rule. Let’s leave it there. The is no national interest in LNG by rail, nor in LNG export. There is no “energy emergency” for fossil fuels.

The recommended response for fire companies and first responders is to try to evacuate and let the fire burn. Imagine the catastrophe in a populated region and around vulnerable and essential infrastructure.
There is no economic or logistical need for transporting LNG by rail car. LNG facilities in operation fulfill the market for LNG exports already; export is the primary market for LNG. The projects under construction and in process of permitting add so much more LNG that a glut of U.S. LNG could turn capital investments into stranded assets. None of these projects require LNG transport by rail car because the practice is to bring in fossil gas in a gaseous state, then liquefy it at the export terminal, loading into marine vessels for export. There is also a downside to the increase in LNG exports for domestic users. “As LNG exports have grown, consumer costs for gas have spiked as well. In early 2021, winter storm Uri caused a supply shock that sent natural gas prices from $3 to $1200 per thousand cubic feet, as a Texas freeze also slashed production. Later, the invasion of Ukraine set off a price war between domestic consumers and gas exporters, sending U.S. gas prices to their highest level in a decade”. The economic forecast for U.S. LNG exports is dim as nations turn to homegrown, sustainable and renewable sources of energy to avoid the high prices of US LNG and to obtain energy security that they can control. This forecast does not support the concept that LNG transport by rail car is needed or justified.
LNG is too volatile and dangerous to allow its bulk transport on railroads where so many variables can lead to disaster. We saw firsthand what a rail accident involving hazardous materials could entail when a train carrying volatile vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio in 2023. That derailment led to several tense days where residents living in the vicinity had to be evacuated and toxic chemicals burned off into the air for fear of an explosion. And the impacts were not just local; the accident resulted in toxic chemicals spreading to sixteen nearby states.
